newsitem.title: USA: Nine West says SEC probe focuses on U.S. Shoe business.
newsitem.headline: Nine West says SEC probe focuses on U.S. Shoe business.

text.p: Nine West Group Inc. said Wednesday a Securities and Exchange Commission inquiry into its accounting practices involves events that took place in 1995 when it acquired U.S. Shoe Corp.'s footwear business.

Nine West, seeking to control damage from its disclosure Tuesday that it was the target of an SEC probe, said "as far as we're aware of at this time" the investigation is isolated to U.S. Shoe's revenue-booking policies two years ago.
"We've stated that we believe that the issues relate to 1995," said Robert Galvin, Nine West's chief financial officer, during a call with investors and reporters.
Stamford, Conn.-based Nine West acquired U.S. Shoe's footwear group in May 1995 for $560 million.
Nine West has about 13,000 employees and operates 1,061 of its own retail stores. Its brands include Enzo Angiolini, Easy Spirit, Bandolino and Evan Picone.
On Tuesday, Nine West disclosed the SEC was probing its revenue accounting policies, and its shares tumbled 18 percent.

They recovered about 5 percent on Wednesday, rising by $1.625 to $34.125 on the New York Stock Exchange, after it said the probe seems to involve U.S. Shoe's accounting practices before it was acquired by Nine West.

Galvin said Nine West has not changed its outlook for the company to report an increase in first-quarter earnings, has no current plans to restate previous results and does not expect the probe to have a material adverse effect on the company's finances.

Wall Street analysts estimate Nine West will report earnings of 47 cents a share for the first quarter later this month, according to First Call. Galvin said it expects the results to be "in line with Street expectations."
Last year, Nine West earned $15.1 million, or 41 cents a share, in the first quarter.

"I think the stock is up because people are looking at the investigation as associated with one year and related to an acquisition, so they know the whole company isn't a bad apple," said Hank Wilson of Hambrecht & Quist.
But Wall Street analysts said until they know more about the scope of the inquiry, they would not recommend purchase of Nine West shares.
During the conference call, Nine West said the SEC launched an informal probe last fall and decided to make it formal in April, a change Nine West was told of last week.

"We have no idea at this point in time when it will be completed," Galvin said. In addition, the SEC has not ruled out widening the investigation to matters other than revenue accounting practices, he added.

Nine West is cooperating with the SEC, he said. The probe has not reached the stage of negotiations, and the company is not aware of what triggered the SEC's decision to make the investigation a formal one.
"It appears the investigation is isolated to 1995," said Jeffrey Stein of McDonald & Co. "But there's nothing to say the scope of the investigation will not be expanded."
